hero.title: Where We Live
hero.description: Kidney disease is shaped by more than genetics — including place, access, and lived experience. We map the structural factors that determine who gets sick and who gets care.
hero.missionStatement: A public accountability platform that connects data with human experience.
hero.missionBody1: Numbers can tell us what is happening. Stories explain why. By pairing datasets with real stories from patients and families living in the Bronx, we see something different. The rates become human. The percentages become people.
hero.missionBody2: This is how we build accountability. This is how we change systems.
hero.pillar1Desc: Geographic data reveals patterns of disease burden, care access, environmental exposure, and structural inequality across neighborhoods.
hero.pillar2Desc: Patient and caregiver stories grounded in place show what the data cannot: lived experience, context, and human reality.
hero.pillar3Desc: When data and stories converge, systems change. Researchers, clinicians, and policymakers can see clearly and respond accordingly.
hero.ctaDesc: Start with the map to see how place shapes disease burden. Then read stories to understand why it matters.

map.title: Map Explorer
map.description: Explore APOL1 and FSGS context by neighborhood. Use the data layers to visualize disease burden, care access, environmental exposure, and area deprivation. Click a ZIP code to see detailed metrics and patient stories.
map.tip: Toggle data layers to compare how different factors correlate with kidney disease burden in each neighborhood.
map.clickNeighborhood: Click a neighborhood on the map to see its profile
map.noLayerSelected: Check a layer above to see its description.
map.dataDisclaimerText: Some layers use proxy or modeled data and do not represent direct clinical measurements. They reflect structural conditions, not individual outcomes or causation.
map.costBurdenDesc: TCOL-based cost burden ratio — required income divided by median income. Values above 1.0 mean basic needs exceed what most households earn. Blue = manageable, red = severe.
map.diseaseBurdenDesc: Proxy for structural risk using HUD tract weight. Not a direct measure of disease prevalence — reflects geographic concentration of structural conditions.
map.careAccessDesc: Proxy for access constraints using HUD residential tract weight. Not a direct measure of care availability — reflects residential distribution across tracts.
map.environmentalDesc: Estimated environmental context derived from tract weight and location. Modeled approximation — not a measured environmental dataset.
map.adiDesc: Census-based composite of income, education, employment, and housing at the block-group level. Purple indicates high deprivation. Real data — University of Wisconsin NNHC 2022.

stories.title: Patient Stories
stories.description: These stories represent patterns documented across communities. Names and identifying details are composite, but the structural barriers they face are real.
stories.wouldChange: What would have changed his outcome:
stories.shouldKnow: What he wishes he had known:
stories.shareDesc: This is for patients and caregivers living with APOL1-mediated kidney disease or FSGS. Your submission is anonymous by default and grounded in neighborhood.
stories.reflectionPlaceholder: How does where you live affect your kidney care? What do clinicians misunderstand about your environment?
stories.privacyNote: Don't include names, exact addresses, employer details, or anything identifying.
stories.consent: I consent to Where We Live using this anonymous submission in aggregated form by place and theme. My story may appear alongside others from my neighborhood when patterns emerge.
stories.howStep1: You select your neighborhood and respond to guided prompts
stories.howStep2: Submissions are reviewed for safety and clarity
stories.howStep3: Stories are grouped by place and theme
stories.howStep4: Individual entries appear only when patterns emerge (minimum threshold)
stories.howStep5: Your voice becomes structural evidence, not isolated testimony

about.openingHeading: tories are the engine that keep human beings moving forward.
about.para1: They inform us. They inspire us. And at times, they make us uncomfortable—forcing us to confront truths we might otherwise avoid.
about.para2: Stories are the thread that holds together the fabric of the American experience. They are how we come to understand who we are, where we come from, and what we are responsible for.
about.para3: From Down These Mean Streets, where a young man made the streets of Spanish Harlem visible to those who had never seen them, to To Kill a Mockingbird, where the moral clarity of Atticus Finch forced a nation to confront its conscience. Through the work of Toni Morrison, who did not allow history to be simplified or forgotten, and even through the voice of Richard Pryor, who told the truth in ways others could not.
about.para4: These stories did not just inform. They shifted perspective. They expanded what people were willing to see—and therefore what they were willing to change.
about.quote1a: Because stories do something data alone cannot.
about.quote1b: They make us feel. And in doing so, they make us care.
about.belief: This project is built on that belief.
about.storiesHealthcareBody: In healthcare, data is essential—but it is often incomplete. Numbers can tell us what is happening, but rarely why. They can show patterns, but they cannot explain lived experience. Patient stories fill that gap. They provide context—cultural, emotional, environmental—that clinical data alone cannot capture. Research increasingly shows that storytelling improves understanding, builds trust, and leads to more patient-centered care. It helps researchers and clinicians align their work with what actually matters in people's lives.
about.storiesHealthcareBody2: For communities affected by kidney disease—particularly those living with FSGS and APOL1-mediated kidney disease—this gap is even more pronounced.
about.question1: What does it mean to manage a chronic disease while living in a neighborhood with limited access to healthy food?
about.question2: What does it mean to navigate treatment while dealing with financial instability or housing insecurity?
about.question3: What does structural racism do—not just to access to care—but to the body itself?
about.questionsNote: These are not abstract questions. They are lived realities.
about.missionBody1: The Rare Renal Equity Project exists to connect these realities to the data. We are not just mapping disease—we are mapping experience. By pairing datasets with real stories from patients and families, we begin to see something different. The numbers stop being distant. They become human.
about.missionBody2: You are no longer looking at a rate, a percentage, or a cluster on a map. You are seeing a person. A family. A set of choices shaped by constraints. A life.
about.missionBody3: Because when we see the human story behind the data, it changes how we respond. Stories make information more memorable, more actionable, and more likely to influence behavior and decision-making. They create connection. They create urgency. They create accountability.
about.missionGoal: Our goal is not just to tell stories, but to make them count.
about.scienceBody1: When you listen to a story, your brain does something remarkable. Brain imaging shows that the listener's brain waves actually synchronize with the storyteller's. It's as though the storyteller is trying to "make your brain similar to mine in areas that really capture the meaning, the situation, the schema—the context of the world."
about.scienceBody2: Different regions light up—not just those involved in language processing, but networks that handle emotions, predict what will happen next, and imagine another person's motives and perspective. Your palms may sweat. You'll blink faster. Your heart might flutter. You become physically immersed in someone else's experience.
about.scienceBody3: Research shows that stories wield a particularly strong influence over our attitudes and behavior. When you read about someone you identify with making a change, you're more likely to make it yourself. When you hear a story rather than a lecture or list of facts, the information feels more real, more important, more personal. It hits you in the heart.
about.scienceQuote: Messages that feel like commands aren't always received well. But when someone tells you a story about their struggle, the information comes across less like a lecture and more like a personal truth. That matters.
about.integratingBody: We believe these stories can be studied, measured, and integrated into how research is done, how care is delivered, and how policy is shaped. This is about putting a human imprint on systems that have historically operated without one. It is about ensuring that when decisions are made—about funding, about research priorities, about care delivery—the voices of those most affected are not an afterthought, but a starting point.
about.ctaDesc: See how patients and families navigate kidney disease while facing structural barriers to care, resources, and health.

methods.title: Methods & Transparency
methods.subtitle: Everything we show is built on explicit, auditable decisions. Here's how we work.
methods.osmDesc: Fast food, liquor stores, grocery access, transit (aggregated)
methods.patientStoriesDesc: Anonymous submissions tied to neighborhood, reviewed for safety
methods.minCellSizeDesc: Metrics with n < 11 are suppressed (NCHS standard)
methods.geoDowngradeDesc: If insufficient data at tract level, aggregate to county
methods.storyThresholdDesc: Stories show only when 5+ submissions from same area/theme
methods.noIndividualDesc: Data never presented in ways that could re-identify people
methods.whatWeShowTitle: What We Show & What We Don't
methods.weDontShow7: Any data that could re-identify people
methods.governanceBody: We are built to be auditable. Every data suppression decision, every story threshold, every narrative choice is logged and explainable.
methods.irbDesc: All data governance rules follow NCHS guidelines and are suitable for IRB scrutiny.
methods.auditDesc: Every governance decision — suppression, downgrading, narrative approval — is logged with timestamp and reasoning.
methods.communityDesc: Rules are designed with community partners, researchers, and funders.

kidney.whatIsPara1: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) happens when the kidneys are damaged for more than a few months. Think of your kidneys as your body's filtration system—they clean the blood by removing waste and extra fluid, which then leaves the body as urine.
kidney.whatIsPara2: But kidneys do much more than just filter waste. They also:
kidney.whatIsItem2: Balance salt and minerals in your blood
kidney.whatIsItem3: Help your body make red blood cells
kidney.whatIsPara3: When kidneys are damaged, they can't do these jobs properly. Waste and fluid build up in your body, which can cause serious health problems.
kidney.whatIsImportant: Important: In the early stages of kidney disease, you might not feel sick or have any symptoms. You might not know that you have kidney disease until the condition is advanced. This is why regular check-ups are important, especially if you have risk factors like high blood pressure or diabetes.
kidney.howFoundTitle: How Do Doctors Find Kidney Disease?
kidney.howFoundPara1: Healthcare professionals can find kidney disease through blood and urine tests. These tests look for:
kidney.howFoundItem1: High levels of waste in the blood
kidney.howFoundItem2: Protein in the urine (which shouldn't normally be there)
kidney.howFoundItem3: Tiny amounts of blood in the urine
kidney.howFoundPara2: Doctors might also use imaging tests like:
kidney.howFoundItem4: Ultrasound: Creates pictures of your kidneys using sound waves
kidney.howFoundItem5: CT scans: Take detailed X-ray images to look at the kidneys in detail
kidney.stagesTitle: The Five Stages of Kidney Disease
kidney.stagesPara1: Your healthcare team determines what stage you have by performing a blood test called the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). This test measures how much blood your kidneys filter each minute. A low eGFR number means your kidneys are working less well.
kidney.stage3aFunc: Mild to moderate loss of kidney function
kidney.stage3bFunc: Moderate to severe loss of kidney function
kidney.stagesPara2: When the kidneys no longer work at the level needed to keep a person alive, it's called end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). This happens when you have an eGFR under 15. At this point, a person needs either a kidney transplant or dialysis (a treatment that does the job of the kidneys).
kidney.symptomsPara1: Chronic kidney disease symptoms tend to develop slowly over time. In the early stages, you might not notice anything at all. This is why many people don't realize they have kidney disease until it's advanced.
kidney.symptomsWhy: Why symptoms develop: Loss of kidney function causes a buildup of fluid or waste in your body. It also can cause acids, potassium, and phosphate to build up in the blood—all of which can cause symptoms.
kidney.symptomsWhen: When symptoms appear: Most people with kidney disease have no symptoms until the very last stages, known as advanced kidney disease.
kidney.symptomsAdvanced: Symptoms of advanced kidney disease include:
kidney.symptomItem6: High blood pressure that's hard to manage
kidney.symptomItem7: Shortness of breath (if fluid builds up in the lungs)
kidney.treatmentPara1: The goal of treatment is to slow down damage to the kidneys. This is often done by managing the underlying cause of the damage—for example, controlling blood pressure or managing diabetes.
kidney.treatmentPara2: However, even after a cause has been found and treated, kidney damage could still get worse. This is why it's important to:
kidney.treatItem5: Work closely with your healthcare team
kidney.eskdTitle: If Kidney Disease Progresses to End-Stage
kidney.eskdDesc: Chronic kidney disease can progress to end-stage kidney failure. This is fatal unless a person gets a kidney transplant or starts dialysis—a treatment that does the job of the kidneys.
kidney.whenSeePara1: If you have an ongoing health condition that raises your risk of kidney disease, your main healthcare professional may want to monitor the health of your kidneys. Risk factors include:
kidney.monitorItem1: Blood tests to check kidney function (eGFR)
kidney.monitorItem2: Urine tests to check for protein
kidney.whenSeePara2: You may see your main healthcare professional every 6 to 12 months for these tests. If test results show possible kidney problems, you may be referred to a nephrologist—a doctor who specializes in kidney diseases.
kidney.typesPara1: Chronic kidney disease can result from many different causes. The type you have affects how it's treated. Some specific types of kidney disease include:
kidney.apol1TypeDesc: A genetic form of kidney disease caused by variations in the APOL1 gene, particularly common in people with African ancestry.
kidney.fsgsTypeDesc: A kidney disease characterized by scarring of the glomeruli (tiny filtering units) and can be caused by various conditions.
kidney.otherTypesDesc: Other types include diabetic kidney disease, lupus nephritis, polycystic kidney disease, and kidney disease from high blood pressure. Your doctor can explain which type you have and what it means for your treatment.
kidney.bottomLineDesc: Kidney disease often has no symptoms in early stages, making regular check-ups essential if you have risk factors. The good news is that treatment can slow disease progression, especially when started early. Work with your healthcare team to monitor your kidney health and manage any underlying conditions.

apol1.overviewPara1: APOL1-mediated kidney disease is a genetic condition that increases the risk of developing chronic kidney disease and kidney failure. It is caused by specific genetic variations (called G1 and G2) in a gene that your body uses to fight certain infections.
apol1.overviewPara2: These genetic variations are particularly common in people with African ancestry, including African Americans, people from the Caribbean, and people from Brazil. This doesn't mean everyone with these variations will develop kidney disease, but they have a higher risk than others.
apol1.overviewPara3: The interesting thing about this genetic condition is that the same gene variations that put you at risk for kidney disease actually protected your ancestors from a serious tropical disease called sleeping sickness. This explains why these variations are so common in certain populations—your ancestors who had them were more likely to survive that disease.
apol1.g1g2Para1: G1 and G2 are two different variations in the APOL1 gene. Think of them as two different "typos" in the same instruction manual for your body. They're different typos, but they both can cause similar problems.
apol1.howGenesPara: You inherit genes from both your mother and father. For most genes, you get one copy from each parent. If you inherit the same variation (like G1 or G2) from both parents, that's when it can affect your health. If you only get it from one parent, you're usually protected.
apol1.g1g2Stats: The numbers tell the story: About 20-22% of African Americans carry the G1 variation, and about 13-15% carry the G2 variation. This means approximately 10-15% of African Americans carry two copies of these variations (one from each parent), putting them at higher risk for kidney disease.
apol1.g1g2Key: The key point: You need to inherit these variations from both parents for them to significantly increase your risk of kidney disease. If you only inherited one from one parent, your risk is much lower.
apol1.whyCommonTitle: Why Is This More Common in African Populations?
apol1.whyCommonPara1: These gene variations are most common in West Africa (in countries like Ghana and Nigeria) and are found throughout sub-Saharan Africa. They arrived in the Americas through the forced migration of millions of Africans during the slave trade.
apol1.whyCommonPara2: The reason these variations became so common in Africa is evolution. Thousands of years ago, when sleeping sickness was a deadly disease that killed many people in Africa, those who carried the G1 or G2 variations had a survival advantage—they were protected from the disease. So they were more likely to survive and have children, passing the variation on to the next generation.
apol1.whyCommonPara3: Over many generations, these protective variations became very common. But the trade-off is that when someone inherits two copies (one from each parent), the same genes that protected their ancestors from a tropical disease now put them at risk for kidney disease. This is a common pattern in human genetics—what protects you in one situation can harm you in another.
apol1.whoAtRiskPara1: APOL1-mediated kidney disease primarily affects people with recent African ancestry, including:
apol1.riskItem5: Anyone with a family history of kidney disease and African heritage
apol1.whoAtRiskNote: Important: Just because you have African ancestry doesn't mean you have these genetic variations. And even if you do, not everyone develops kidney disease. About 70-85% of African Americans do not carry two copies of these variations.
apol1.testingAdvice: Who should get tested? If you're planning to donate a kidney and have African ancestry, your doctor may recommend testing for APOL1 variations as part of your evaluation.
apol1.problemsTitle: What Kidney Problems Can APOL1 Cause?
apol1.problemsPara1: APOL1-mediated kidney disease can cause several different types of kidney problems, including:
apol1.problemItem1: HIV-associated kidney disease (HIVAN): People with HIV who also carry two APOL1 variations have a very high risk of developing kidney damage
apol1.problemItem2: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS): A type of kidney scarring (see FSGS page for more details)
apol1.problemItem3: Kidney disease related to lupus or sickle cell disease: For people with these conditions, having APOL1 variations increases their risk of severe kidney problems
apol1.problemItem4: High blood pressure-related kidney disease: APOL1 variations can make hypertension more damaging to the kidneys
apol1.problemItem5: Chronic kidney disease (CKD): General decline in kidney function over time
apol1.problemsKey: The key point: Having APOL1 variations doesn't guarantee you'll get kidney disease, but it does increase your risk—sometimes dramatically. Studies show that people with two copies of these variations develop kidney problems and progress to kidney failure much faster than those without them.
apol1.progressionTitle: How Fast Does APOL1 Kidney Disease Progress?
apol1.progressionPara1: The speed of progression varies from person to person. However, research shows that people with two APOL1 variations tend to develop kidney problems 5-10 years earlier than people without them.
apol1.progressionPara2: For example, if someone without APOL1 variations might need dialysis at age 60, someone with two copies might need it at age 50-55. This means starting kidney protective treatments earlier is especially important if you have these variations.
apol1.progressionGoodNews: The good news: Controlling blood pressure and managing other conditions (like diabetes or HIV) can slow the progression and delay the need for dialysis or transplant.
apol1.donationPara1: If you're considering donating a kidney and have African ancestry, your doctor may test you for APOL1 variations. This is important because:
apol1.donationItem1: Donors with two APOL1 variations have a higher risk of developing kidney disease after donation than donors without these variations
apol1.donationItem2: Your doctor needs this information to help you understand your personal risk and make an informed decision about donation
apol1.donationItem3: The benefits of kidney donation to the recipient usually still outweigh these risks, but you and your doctor should discuss what's right for your situation
apol1.donationKey: The important thing: Having APOL1 variations doesn't automatically disqualify you from donating. Instead, it means your medical team will monitor you more closely after donation and work with you on strategies to protect your remaining kidney.
apol1.testingPara1: APOL1 testing is a simple genetic test done with a blood sample or saliva. It can tell you:
apol1.testingItem1: Whether you carry zero, one, or two copies of the G1 or G2 variations
apol1.testingItem2: Your overall risk level for kidney disease
apol1.testingRecommended: Currently, routine testing is recommended mainly for:
apol1.testRec1: People considering kidney donation (especially those with African ancestry)
apol1.testRec2: People with African ancestry who have kidney disease and want to understand their risk factors
apol1.testRec3: Patients with HIV who have African ancestry
apol1.whatCanPara1: If you have APOL1 variations, here are things you can do to protect your kidney health:
apol1.preventItem1: Control your blood pressure: This is the single most important thing you can do. Keep your blood pressure at your doctor's target level
apol1.preventItem2: Manage diabetes: If you have diabetes, tight control of blood sugar helps protect your kidneys
apol1.preventItem3: Avoid certain medications: NSAIDs (like ibuprofen) can damage kidneys, especially for people with APOL1 variations
apol1.preventItem4: Maintain a healthy weight: Obesity increases kidney stress
apol1.preventItem5: Exercise regularly: Physical activity helps protect your heart and kidneys
apol1.preventItem6: Eat a healthy diet: Low sodium, appropriate protein intake
apol1.preventItem7: Avoid smoking: Smoking damages blood vessels, including those in your kidneys
apol1.preventItem8: Get regular kidney health check-ups: Regular blood and urine tests help catch problems early
apol1.futureTreatmentsDesc: Researchers are working on new medications specifically designed to treat APOL1 kidney disease. Early studies show promise, including a drug called inaxaplin that may slow kidney damage. Ask your doctor about clinical trials that might be available to you.
apol1.keyItem1: APOL1 kidney disease is genetic, but you only have higher risk if you inherited the variation from both parents
apol1.keyItem2: These variations are common in people with African ancestry, but not everyone with African ancestry has them
apol1.keyItem3: Having the variation doesn't mean you will definitely get kidney disease—it just means your risk is higher
apol1.keyItem4: Blood pressure control is your best defense against developing kidney disease if you have APOL1 variations
apol1.keyItem5: Regular kidney monitoring is important if you have two copies of these variations
apol1.keyItem6: Talk to your doctor about your risk if you have African ancestry and kidney disease, or if you're considering kidney donation

fsgs.overviewPara1: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is a disease in which scar tissue develops on the glomeruli—the small parts of the kidneys that filter waste from the blood. Glomeruli are the tiny filtering units inside your kidney where blood is cleaned of wastes and toxins.
fsgs.overviewPara2: FSGS is a serious condition that can lead to kidney failure, which can only be treated with dialysis or kidney transplant. Only some glomeruli are affected, but over time FSGS can lead to progressive kidney damage. You may experience swelling, have foamy urine and feel rundown due to the buildup of toxins in your body.
fsgs.overviewPara3: Treatment options for FSGS depend on the type you have and can help slow ongoing kidney damage and might lead to improved kidney function over time.
fsgs.primaryDesc: Many people diagnosed with FSGS have no known cause for their condition. This is called primary (idiopathic) FSGS.
fsgs.secondaryDesc: Several factors can cause secondary FSGS, including infections, drug toxicity, diseases (such as diabetes or sickle cell disease), obesity, and other kidney diseases. Controlling or treating the underlying cause often slows ongoing kidney damage and might lead to improved kidney function over time.
fsgs.geneticPara1: This is a rare form of FSGS caused by genetic changes, also called familial FSGS. It's suspected when several members of a family show signs of FSGS.
fsgs.geneticPara2: Familial FSGS can also occur when neither parent has the disease but each one carries a copy of an altered gene that can be passed on to the next generation.
fsgs.unknownDesc: In some cases, the underlying cause of FSGS cannot be determined despite the evaluation of clinical symptoms and extensive testing.
fsgs.symptomsPara1: Many people with FSGS have no symptoms at all. When symptoms are present, they might include:
fsgs.symptomItem1: Swelling (edema) in the legs and ankles, around the eyes, and in other body parts
fsgs.seeDoctor: When to see a doctor: Contact your healthcare provider if you have any of the symptoms of FSGS.
fsgs.causesPara1: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) can be caused by a variety of conditions:
fsgs.causeItem1: Medical conditions including diabetes, sickle cell disease, lupus, and other kidney diseases
fsgs.causeItem3: Infections such as HIV and hepatitis C
fsgs.causeItem4: Damage from illicit drugs, medicines, or toxins
fsgs.causeItem5: Gene changes passed through families (inherited gene changes) that can cause a rare form of FSGS
fsgs.causeItem6: Sometimes there is no known cause
fsgs.riskPara1: Factors that can raise your risk of developing FSGS include:
fsgs.riskItem1: Medical conditions that can damage the kidneys such as diabetes, lupus, obesity, and other kidney diseases
fsgs.riskItem2: Certain infections including HIV and hepatitis C
fsgs.riskItem3: Gene changes passed through families that can raise the risk of FSGS
fsgs.riskItem4: Demographics: Males more than females; adults age 45 and older most prevalent; more common in people of African American descent
fsgs.diagnosisPara1: If your healthcare provider suspects FSGS, they will review your medical history and order some tests such as:
fsgs.diagItem1: Blood tests: Check kidney function and protein levels
fsgs.diagItem2: Urine tests: Look for protein (proteinuria) and blood in urine
fsgs.diagItem3: Kidney biopsy: A small sample of kidney tissue is examined under a microscope to confirm the diagnosis and determine the type of FSGS
fsgs.medsPara1: Several medications can help manage FSGS symptoms and slow progression:
fsgs.medItem1: ACE inhibitors or ARBs: Lower blood pressure and reduce protein in urine
fsgs.medItem2: Corticosteroids: Reduce inflammation in the kidneys
fsgs.medItem3: Immunosuppressants: Suppress the immune response attacking the kidneys
fsgs.medItem4: Diuretics: Help manage swelling and fluid retention
fsgs.lifestylePara1: Important lifestyle modifications that can help support healthy kidneys:
fsgs.lifestyleItem2: Follow a low sodium / low protein diet
fsgs.lifestyleItem4: Avoid medications that can harm kidneys (such as NSAIDs)
fsgs.lifestyleItem6: Take daily vitamins (such as Vitamin D)
fsgs.shortTermGoals: Short-term goals: Reduce proteinuria, control blood pressure, manage swelling
fsgs.longTermGoals: Long-term goals: Preserve kidney function, prevent progression to kidney failure, maintain quality of life
fsgs.complicationsPara1: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) may lead to other health concerns, including:
fsgs.nephroticDesc: This kidney condition causes the body to pass too much protein in the urine. Nephrotic syndrome raises the risk of other health conditions, such as blood clots and high blood pressure.
fsgs.failurePara1: Damage to the kidneys that can't be fixed causes the kidneys to stop working. The only treatments for kidney failure are dialysis or kidney transplant.
fsgs.dialysisDesc: Dialysis: A mechanical process that filters waste and excess fluid from your blood
fsgs.transplantDesc: Kidney transplant: Receiving a healthy kidney from a donor
fsgs.journeyDesc: The FSGS journey is unique for each patient. Close follow-up care with your healthcare provider is extremely important to help maintain the health of your kidneys and manage your condition effectively.
